fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Verse 125 says, “I am Your servant; give me understanding, that I may know Your testimonies.” He starts with who he is, the LORD's servant. Then he asks for understanding so he can know the testimonies. That's a servant asking for exactly what he needs.
I can see how that sounds smooth, baker, but it's not what he says. Verse 128 says he admires all the precepts “…and hate every false way.” The word there is hate. Follows isn't in the verse.

That's right, baker. Verse 130 says, “The unfolding of Your words gives light; it informs the simple.” You don't have to be fancy for it to work. I think that's good news for anybody who's ever felt a little worn down, and I've been a worn-down stamper myself.

Strong guess, friend, but I don't see the mighty anywhere in this verse. The light of God's words goes to somebody else. Verse 130 says, “The unfolding of Your words gives light; it informs the simple.” Simple is the word.

Yes, baker. Verse 134 says, “Redeem me from the oppression of man, that I may keep Your precepts.” Look at the order. First he asks to be redeemed, and then he says why: so he can keep the precepts. I think a man asking for rescue and a chance to keep the LORD's word in the same breath knows what he cares about.

I get it, friend, but questions isn't the word in the verse. Verse 140 says, “Your promise is completely pure; therefore Your servant loves it.” The servant's word for the promise is love. That therefore connects the two.

That's right, baker. Verse 142 says, “Your righteousness is everlasting and Your law is true.” Everlasting means it never ends. I'd say that's worth a happy dance, and I'm doing one on my gold base right now.

That's a believable guess with trouble in the picture, baker. But verse 143 says, “Trouble and distress have found me, but Your commandments are my delight.” Notice the “but.” Trouble has found him, and in the same breath he calls the commandments his delight.

Yes, baker. Verse 144 says, “Your testimonies are righteous forever. Give me understanding, that I may live.” He asked for understanding back in verse 125 too, so this is the second time he asks. I think that tells you how much he wants it.

Winning would be fun, friend, but nobody's keeping score in this verse. The psalmist says the testimonies are righteous forever, and then he asks for understanding. Verse 144 says he wants it “…that I may live.” That's his reason, and I think it's a big one.
